In Wikisubmission, you do not manually label the data. Instead, we label the dataset using wikilabeling sources such as simple heuristic rules, knowledge bases or locality codes. As illustrated in the figure on the right, when compared to human notations, the weak annotations are much cheaper. Yet they are also noisy, meaning that a certain amount of the annotations are incorrect. If we directly train neural networks on weekly label data, the neural networks tend to memorize the label noise and do not generalize. In weekly supervised learning algorithms are proposed. Train neural networks under such label noise, so that the trained models still generalize well. In recent works in WSL, so WSL stands for weakly supervised learning. Common claim is that people say that the only trimodels on the weekly labeled it and achieve high performance on clean test sets. Technically, this claim is not wrong but there's a catch. People do assume that there is an additional clean validation set or well-formed model selection. We cast doubt on this problem setting, as it implies that additional manual annotations are required in I say, but like an elephant in the room. This necessity is often overlooked. The affirmation adopted is us to ask three. Questions: First, is clean validation data necessary for WPSL? Or can we maybe use the noisy validation set instead? Second, if clean data is required or if clean dataset is mandatory. Out to work, then home. Many clean samples do we need? Finally, should we only use the clean samples for validation or there are better ways to utilize them? These research questions in our work and our findings are as follows: First, we find that interestingly recent TPSL methods indeed require clean water-based samples to work properly. Otherwise, there is a large performance drop. As shown in this figure: if there are no clean validation samples, then the trained models cannot generalize beyond the original big labels, meaning that of training is pointless. That WSL approaches actually require cleanly labeled data to work properly, and the annotation cost for obtaining clean validation samples should not be overlooked. Our second finding is that increasing the number of clean validation samples will help WSL approaches to achieve better performance, as shown in the figure on the left. We only need twenty samples per class to attain high performance. But that's not the end of the story, because if we either way decide to access clean samples, then training on them directly will. Better performance. Finally, the performance improvement claimed in previous. As our approaches can be easily achieved by allowing to continue fine tuning on the clean validation samples, as we can see from the figures.
